blind_target.title: Eighteen-month-old infants show false belief understanding in an active helping paradigm.

blind_target.title: Do 15-month-old infants understand false beliefs?
blind_target.evidence_quote: We conducted close replications of studies by Knudsen and Liszkowski (2012) and Buttelmann et al. (2009), as well as two experiments based on published violation of expectation paradigms (Onishi & Baillargeon, 2005; Song, Onishi, Baillargeon & Fisher, 2008; Träuble, Marinović & Pauen, 2010), with procedural changes based on both our novel experimental goals and the original authors’ advice.
blind_target.outcome_quote: On the other hand, we failed to reproduce evidence that 18-month-old infants’ expectations are violated when an experimenter who ought to have a false belief reaches for an object in its true location (e.g. Onishi & Baillargeon, 2005; Song et al., 2008; Träuble et al., 2010).
blind_target.outcome_reasoning: Author verdict explicitly identifies this original; limitations do not replace that verdict.

luna_triage.reason: Experiment 1 Task 1 directly retests the false-belief helping finding from Buttelmann et al. The results report that infants selected the toy's actual location as in the original; the General Discussion explicitly says this finding was replicated. The only supplied shipped original is Knudsen and Liszkowski (2011/2012), a different paper.
luna_triage.location: Experiment 1, Task 1 Results; General Discussion; References
luna_triage.omission_quote: Fifty-nine of the 94 participants (62.8%) first touched or opened the box containing the tiger; the remaining 35 first touched or opened the empty box E1 acted on. This distribution differed significantly from chance (z(93) = 2.37, P < 0.05). Thus, as in Buttelmann and colleagues’ original study (2009), 1.5-year-old infants were more likely to help not by opening the box the experimenter was pulling on, but by retrieving the toy the experimenter falsely believed to be in that box.
